unit.title: Develop and monitor financial policy statements and operating procedures

summary: This unit teaches you to develop financial policy statements and the operating procedures that put them into practice, and to monitor whether they are followed. You will learn how to identify the need for a policy, check the law and other rules, consult the people affected, draft clear wording, get approval, introduce the policy with training, measure compliance, deal with breaches and review the policy when things change.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is for supervisors and managers in Jamaican companies, hotels, schools, co-operatives and public bodies who write, introduce or enforce the rules for handling money and assets. You will **develop** policies and procedures (find the need, draft, consult, approve) and **monitor** them (check that people follow them, deal with breaches, review and improve).

A **financial policy statement** sets out the rules and principles for handling money and assets, and the reasons for them. An **operating procedure** explains, step by step, how the policy is carried out: who does what, with which form, by when. Policy says **what** and **why**; procedure says **how**.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workplace
rows: Recognise why a policy is needed (audit finding, growth, a loss, a change in the law) and what it must achieve.
Check company and tax law, public finance and procurement rules, record-keeping rules and existing policies.
Involve the people who will use or be affected by the policy, and test the draft against real cases.
Write clear, usable, enforceable policies with purpose, scope, definitions, rules, roles and a review date.
Write numbered steps, draw flowcharts and design forms that put the policy into practice.
Obtain approval from the right body, control versions, communicate, train and start on a sensible date.
Use exception reports, sample tests, compliance rates and audit findings to see if policies are followed.
Find causes, correct problems, act fairly and update policies when law, systems or risks change.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenarios and short calculations (compliance rates, debtor days, limits, allowances, reserves).
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Group practical tasks**: drafting a travel and expense policy and procedure with a flowchart and sample claims, and testing a set of purchase records for compliance and reporting to a role-played finance committee.

blocks.note: In scenario questions, decide first whether the item is a policy matter (a rule, a limit, a principle) or a procedure matter (a step, a form, a time limit). Then ask who approves it and how compliance will be checked.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Policy, procedure and the documents around them

head: Level
What it is
Example
rows: Set by Parliament or a regulator; the organisation cannot change them
Company law, tax law, public financial management and procurement rules, the data protection law
The organisation's own rules and principles, approved by the board or the head of the body
'All purchases above the approved limit require three written quotations.'
Step-by-step instructions that put the policy into practice
'Step 4: The buyer attaches the three quotations to the requisition and sends it to the budget holder.'
The practical tools used at each step
Requisition form, claim form, quick guide, flowchart

head: Point
Financial policy statement
Operating procedure
rows: What must be done, and why
How, step by step; who; with what; by when
The board, a board committee or the head of the body
Management, within the policy, usually the finance manager or a senior officer
More often, when systems, forms or staff change
'The organisation repays only reasonable costs of approved business travel; receipts are required; no one may approve their own claim.'
'Complete claim form C1; attach receipts; submit to your line manager within 30 days; the manager checks and signs within 5 days; finance pays by transfer.'

blocks.p: An organisation needs **both**. A policy without a procedure gets applied in different ways by different people. A procedure without a policy has no clear authority behind it, and staff can challenge it.

ul: **Consistency:** everyone follows the same rules, so decisions are fair and predictable.
**Control:** limits, approvals and separation of duties are fixed in writing, not left to memory.
**Compliance:** the organisation shows that it follows law and good practice, which auditors, lenders, funders and regulators expect.
**Authority:** staff can point to the policy when they refuse an improper request.
**Continuity:** rules stay in place when people change jobs.
**Training:** new staff learn how things are done.

blocks.p: In a ministry, agency or municipal corporation, financial policies sit inside national public finance and procurement rules, instructions from the Ministry of Finance and the budget approved by Parliament. The organisation's own policies and procedures mostly add local detail. They **cannot be looser** than the national rules. Accountability runs to the head of the body (such as the Permanent Secretary or chief executive), the Auditor General and Parliament, so records and audit trails must be especially complete. A private company has more freedom, but must still follow company and tax law and answer to its board and auditors.

blocks.note: Parish councils were reorganised as municipal corporations in 2016. Their financial rules come from public finance law and instructions, not from the council's own preferences.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Identifying the need and finding the requirements

head: Trigger
Example
rows: The external auditor reports weak cash controls at a hotel
A small firm adds branches and has no written credit rules
Moving to an online accounting system; starting to sell in US dollars
Bad debts double; staff dispute what expenses can be claimed
Request from the board, funder or lender
A donor requires a written reserves policy

blocks.p: Before drafting, define **the need**: the risk or problem, what the policy must achieve, whom it will cover and what success looks like. Use an analysis of the problem and of present practice to see where the **gaps** are. For example, a distributor whose bad debts have doubled should first analyse which customers owe, for how long and why, before writing a credit policy.

head: Source
What to check
rows: Duties of directors; keeping accounting records; filing returns
Tax law and tax authority rules
Records to be kept and for how long; GCT at the current rate; employer deductions and contributions; treatment of allowances
Public finance and procurement rules (public bodies)
Approval limits, quotations and tender rules, reporting; the policy must work within them
Pay, deductions and conditions that affect payroll and expense policies
How personal information in finance records is used, shared and protected
What auditors will expect to see

blocks.p: State requirements by their purpose (for example 'the tax law requires business records to be kept for a set number of years'). Do not guess the period: check the current rule. A policy that tells staff to destroy invoices after one year would be wrong if tax and company rules require a longer period.

blocks.note: Also check the organisation's **other policies**: HR, code of conduct, procurement, IT, risk. A new financial rule must not contradict them. If a gifts and hospitality rule in the purchasing procedure differs from the staff code of conduct, agree one rule with HR and update both documents.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Consult early, and before the draft is final. Good consultation:

ul: improves the policy, because front-line staff know where a step will work or break;
builds support, so staff are more willing to follow the rule;
finds conflicts with other policies and systems.

head: Who
Why consult them
rows: Staff who request, approve, receive, record and pay
They know how the process really works
They carry the budget and must follow the rules
Links to pay, discipline, code of conduct
What the system can enforce or report
Internal audit and the external auditor
Where the rules affect conditions of work
The board or committee that will approve it
They decide, so they should not be surprised

blocks.p: **Test the draft against real cases.** Take a recent claim, purchase or order and walk it through the draft. If staff would read a sentence in different ways, rewrite it.

head: Heading
What it says
rows: So the reader knows which document this is and who keeps it up to date
Why the policy exists, in one or two sentences
What and whom it covers (all staff? contractors? all branches? which money?)
Key terms read in only one way (for example 'business travel', 'budget holder')
The rules, using 'must' for requirements and 'should' for good practice
Who may approve what, up to what amount (a schedule)
Related procedures, forms, laws and other policies
How compliance is checked, and what happens if the policy is broken
Date of the next review and what would trigger an earlier one

blocks.p: Write 'the budget holder approves' or 'the finance manager reviews', not 'Mr Brown approves'. The policy then stays valid when people change jobs. Name a **policy owner** (a role) who keeps it up to date and starts the review.

ul: Say why the policy exists, and whom it covers.
Use plain words and short sentences. Define technical terms.
Be specific: give figures, limits and time periods instead of 'reasonable', 'regularly' or 'as soon as possible'.
Use 'must' (required) and 'should' (recommended) consistently.
State what happens if the policy is not followed.
Keep it as short as it can be: a policy that no one reads is not a control.

head: Poor wording
Why it is poor
Better wording
rows: 'Staff will be repaid sensible hotel costs.'
'Sensible' is a matter of opinion; two officers will decide differently
'Hotel costs are repaid up to the rate in Schedule A, with an itemised receipt.'
'Purchases above J$250,000 must be approved by the department manager before an order is placed.'
Names a person, not a role; fails when he leaves
'Cheques are signed by two authorised signatories from the approved list.'
'Claims must be submitted within 30 days of the trip.'

blocks.h: Delegation of authority: a worked schedule

head: Role
Approves purchases up to
Approves write-off of a bad debt up to

ul: Read across: a J$95,000 write-off is above the finance manager's J$50,000 limit, so the **managing director** approves it.
Splitting one order into smaller ones to stay under a limit is a breach.
Public bodies: limits must stay within national rules.

blocks.note: The schedule makes it clear who has authority, so an approval is valid. Keep it with the policy and update it when roles change.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Common financial policies: what they must contain

blocks.p: You should know the main subjects of financial policies, and be able to do the sums that go with them. The figures below are examples; use the figures in your organisation's policy.

ul: **Who gets credit:** application form, trade and bank references, credit check, set credit limit.
**Terms:** period (for example 30 days), stated on every invoice; any early-payment discount.
**Collection steps:** statement at month end, reminder at a set number of days overdue, call, stop supply, referral for recovery.
**Approval of limits and write-offs** by the delegation schedule.
**Reporting:** a monthly **aged debtors** report and a target for debtor days.

blocks.p: **Debtor days = debtors ÷ credit sales × 365.** A seafood exporter has credit sales of J$18,250,000 a year and debtors of J$2,000,000. Credit sales per day = J$18,250,000 ÷ 365 = J$50,000. Debtor days = J$2,000,000 ÷ J$50,000 = **40 days**. If the terms are 30 days, customers take 10 days longer than agreed.

**Credit limit check.** A customer's limit is J$800,000 and she owes J$650,000. A new order of J$220,000 would take her balance to J$870,000, which is **J$70,000 over** her limit. The policy should say the order is held until an authorised person approves it or she pays down her balance.

ul: Sets the **capitalisation threshold**: items costing at or above it are recorded as assets and depreciated; cheaper items are charged as expenses.
Requires tagging, a fixed asset register with location and custodian, an annual check, and approval for disposals.

blocks.p: **Example.** With a threshold of J$150,000, a printer costing J$120,000 is an **expense**; a photocopier costing J$180,000 is a **fixed asset**. Check the policy wording: some say 'at or above', some 'more than'.

ul: Which costs are repaid (and which are not); rates and limits; approvals in advance; evidence needed (receipts, trip records); time limit for claims; who approves; no self-approval; what happens on a breach.
**Mileage:** staff using their own cars on approved business are paid a rate per kilometre. At an example rate of J$55 per km, a 240 km trip is 240 × J$55 = **J$13,200**.
**Allowances:** a fixed amount per day, for example J$3,800 a day for meals. A 3-day trip pays 3 × J$3,800 = **J$11,400**.

head: Policy
What it should set out
rows: How much cash the body aims to hold, usually as months of operating costs; who may use it. **Example:** four months of yearly operating costs of J$27,000,000: J$27,000,000 ÷ 12 = J$2,250,000 a month; 4 × J$2,250,000 = **J$9,000,000**.
Aims (safety first, then return), approved types of investment, limits and who decides
How exchange rates are chosen for recording, who may buy or sell currency, how currency risk is managed
Float size, receipts, counts, banking intact and daily, safe access
Limits, quotations, tenders, approved suppliers, conflicts of interest; in public bodies, the national rules
Who prepares and approves budgets, how variances are reported and explained
What records are kept, for how long, where and how they are destroyed, as the law requires
Who authorises pay changes; payment dates; deductions
Gifts and hospitality, conflicts of interest
What may be accepted or offered; how it is declared
Zero tolerance; how to report concerns; protection from reprisal

blocks.p: A procedure turns a policy rule into daily action. If staff cannot follow it without asking, it is not ready.

ul: **Purpose and the policy it supports.**
**Roles** by job title, including who covers when the usual person is absent.
**Numbered steps** in the order work is done, each showing who does it, with which form or screen, and the time allowed.
**Controls shown at the step where they happen**: approvals, checks, matching, signatures.
**Exceptions:** what to do when something does not fit (an urgent payment, an unusual claim) and who may approve it.
**Forms and templates** attached.
A **flowchart** of the steps and decisions.
Version number, date, owner and review date.

ol: The claimant completes the claim form and attaches all receipts within 30 days of the trip.
The claimant signs and sends it to the line manager.

The line manager checks that the trip was approved, that receipts are attached and rates are correct, and signs within 5 working days. A manager may not approve his or her own claim; it goes to the next level.
Finance checks arithmetic, coding and limits, and queries any difference with the claimant.
Finance pays by bank transfer to the claimant's own account within 10 working days of receiving the approved claim.
Finance files the claim and reports exceptions each month.

blocks.p: A **flowchart** shows the steps and decisions of a procedure with boxes and arrows. Use a few simple shapes.

head: Shape
Meaning
rows: A decision, with 'yes' and 'no' arrows (for example 'Within limit?')

ul: Show **who** does each step (columns or swim lanes).
Show the approval path **and the rejection path** (what happens if the answer is no).
Make sure the flowchart matches the written steps exactly.

blocks.note: Test the procedure with the staff who will use it. Ask a new clerk to follow the steps with a sample claim and note where they hesitate. Where staff keep breaking a rule because one step takes three days, the **procedure** may be at fault: fix the step, do not just punish the staff.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Approval, version control, communication and implementation

flow: Draft the policy and procedure; consult the people affected
Check the draft against law, other policies, delegation of authority and the systems in use
Prepare a short paper for the approving body: the need, the main rules, the cost of putting it in place, the plan for training
Approval: the board or a committee with that power approves **policies**; management approves **procedures** within them

blocks.p: The finance manager's check before the board sees a draft matters: a policy that conflicts with law or the system will fail in practice.

ul: Every document carries a **version number, date approved, owner and review date**.
There is **one central, controlled copy** (a shared folder or intranet page) that staff can reach.
Old versions are marked 'withdrawn' and removed from use.
A short log records what changed and why.
Printed copies are marked 'uncontrolled if printed'.
Brief the senior team first, so that they lead by example.
Train the staff who request, approve, receive and pay, with real examples and the new forms.
Give a **quick guide** (one page) and a **flowchart**, and name a **contact officer** for questions.
Ask staff to **confirm in writing** that they have read and understood key policies. This gives a record that they were told and supports later action.
Explain **why** each rule exists; people follow rules they understand.

blocks.p: Start only when the system, forms and training are ready. If a new expense policy needs a new claim form in the accounting system, the policy begins when the form is working and staff have been trained, not on the day it was approved. For the first weeks, run a help desk, review early transactions closely and give feedback rather than blame for honest mistakes.

blocks.note: In a public agency with offices in several parishes, hold training in each office, make the documents available in one place and keep to the national procurement rules throughout.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Monitoring compliance and dealing with breaches

blocks.p: A policy that nobody checks is only a hope. Plan the monitoring when you write the policy.

head: Method
What it shows
rows: **Exception reports** from the system (for example payments without a purchase order, claims over limit)
Items that break a rule, listed for a manager to review each month
**Sample tests** against the policy each quarter
The compliance rate, and the kinds of breach
That managers believe they are following the policy
An independent view on whether policies are followed and work
Debtor days and bad debts (credit policy); share of purchases with an approved order (purchasing); claims paid on time
Where the rules are unclear or unworkable

blocks.p: **Compliance rate = items that followed the rule ÷ items tested × 100.**

ul: A sample of 150 expense claims finds 21 that break the policy. Non-compliance = 21 ÷ 150 = 14%. Compliance = **86%**.
A sample of 60 purchase orders finds 45 correctly approved: 45 ÷ 60 = **75%** compliance.

blocks.p: Set a target (for example at least 95% for a basic control), and retest a new sample after the fixes.

blocks.h: Look at the kind of breach, not only the number

blocks.p: In the 21 breaches above, suppose 17 were small claims without receipts and 4 were claims approved by the claimant. The four are much more serious: they break a key control and could hide fraud. Check whether the amounts were genuine, report them to senior management, and deal with them under the policy and the disciplinary rules. Ask also why the system allowed self-approval, and block it.

head: Cause
Response
rows: Staff did not know the rule
A step is slow or unclear
Improve the procedure (for example a faster route for urgent items)
Change the system rule: block, require attachment
Disciplinary action under the policy; report to the committee

ul: Every breach is reported and dealt with under the policy, **whatever the amount and the person's rank**.
Honest mistakes lead to training; deliberate or repeated breaches lead to discipline.
Actions have an owner and a date, and the finance committee sees the results and trends.
Use the evidence in the next review of the policy.

blocks.p: Staff watch what leaders do. If a director skips approvals, claims outside the rules or ignores audit findings, staff learn that the rules are optional. A finance manager builds a culture of compliance by writing clear, practical policies with reasons stated, by asking senior managers to follow the rules visibly, by regular training, by reporting results openly and by providing a safe **whistleblowing** channel for reporting concerns without fear of reprisal.

blocks.note: When a manager approves her own claim, even a small one, the breach is reported. The amount is not the point: the control is.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: On a **regular cycle**, for example every two or three years (or every year for high-risk areas such as cash and payments).
**Sooner** when the law, the rules for public bodies, the systems or the organisation's risks change.
After an audit finding, a fraud, or a series of breaches.
When monitoring shows the rule is unworkable or the compliance rate stays low.

blocks.p: A firm moving from paper invoices to an online accounting system must update its payment procedure to match the new system and its controls.

blocks.h: Planning a review of old policies

flow: List every financial policy and procedure, with owner and date, since you cannot review what you have not found
Check each against current law, rules and systems
Gather evidence: audit findings, exception reports, compliance tests, losses, staff feedback
Rank by risk and agree a timetable with the finance committee; high-risk areas (cash, payments) first
Owners redraft, consult users, remove contradictions, add version control and review dates
Set a review cycle so the problem does not return

blocks.p: After six months, ask: has it done what it was meant to do? For example, a new expense policy may speed up processing, but staff complain about one rule. Collect the evidence (compliance rate, processing time, complaints), review that rule with the staff, and propose a change if the evidence supports it. Policies should be improved, and removed if they no longer add value.

head: Question
Evidence
rows: Changes in law, systems, structure since the last review
Is it consistent with other policies?
Check against HR, procurement, code of conduct

ul: explain the difference between a financial policy and an operating procedure and why both are needed;
say what triggers the need for a new or changed policy;
name the outside requirements to check, including public finance and procurement rules for public bodies;
say whom to consult and why;
lay out a policy statement with purpose, scope, definitions, rules, roles, delegation, links, monitoring and review;
write clear wording, using specific figures and 'must' and 'should';
read a delegation-of-authority schedule and say who approves what;
describe the main subjects of financial policies and do the sums for debtor days, credit limits, thresholds, mileage, allowances and reserves;
write numbered procedure steps and draw a flowchart;
describe approval, version control, communication, training and the start of a new policy;
monitor compliance with exception reports, sample tests and audit, and calculate a compliance rate;
find the cause of a breach and decide a fair response;
decide when and how to review a policy.

terms: The organisation's written rules and principles for handling money and assets, with reasons
Step-by-step instructions that put a policy into practice
What and whom a policy covers
A schedule of who may approve what, up to what amount
The cost above which an item is recorded as a fixed asset, not an expense
A list of what customers owe, grouped by how long it has been owing
A diagram of the steps and decisions of a procedure
Numbering and dating each issue of a document so that only the current one is used
The role responsible for keeping a policy up to date and starting its review
A report listing only items that break a rule or limit
Items that followed the rule ÷ items tested × 100
A function that gives independent assurance on controls and compliance
A protected channel for reporting suspected wrongdoing
A failure to follow a policy or procedure

c1.title: Travel claims at a logistics firm in Portmore
c1.text: A logistics firm in Portmore has no written travel rules; its draft says 'staff will be repaid sensible travel costs'. Sales staff use their own cars on approved visits. The owner proposes a rate of J$55 per kilometre and wants managers to approve their own claims 'to save time'. A salesman, Orville, drove 240 km on an approved visit to Mandeville and Black River and wants to claim.

c2.title: A seafood exporter in Black River sells on credit
c2.text: A seafood exporter in Black River, St Elizabeth, sells to hotels on 30-day terms. Yearly credit sales are J$18,250,000 and debtors are J$2,000,000. One hotel has a credit limit of J$800,000, owes J$650,000 and places a new order for J$220,000. The finance manager is drafting a credit policy. The policy's delegation schedule lets the finance manager write off debts up to J$50,000, the managing director up to J$250,000, and the board above that. A debt of J$95,000 has been judged unrecoverable.

c3.title: A procurement procedure for an agency in Kingston
c3.text: A Kingston agency of a ministry is writing its own purchasing procedure. The first draft lets department heads buy directly, without quotations, up to J$600,000; the national public procurement rules set a lower limit for buying without quotations. The draft is written in long paragraphs, uses the names of current officers, and does not say who acts when a budget holder is on leave. The finance team prepared it alone.

c4.title: A new petty cash policy at a hotel group in Negril
c4.text: A hotel group in Negril introduced a new petty cash and expense policy three months ago. The finance manager tested a sample of 150 claims. Twenty-one broke the policy: 17 were small claims without receipts and 4 were approved by the person claiming. The general manager says senior staff should be exempt from the receipt rule because they are trusted.

c5.title: A school board reviews its policies in Clarendon
c5.text: A school board in Clarendon has not reviewed its financial policies since 2016. Its audit report says the fixed asset register is incomplete. The asset policy sets a capitalisation threshold of J$150,000. The school has just bought a printer costing J$120,000 and a photocopier costing J$180,000. The delegation schedule lets the principal approve purchases up to J$100,000; the board's finance committee approves above that. The principal wants to buy equipment for J$140,000.

questions.q: Which wording for the travel rule is best for the policy statement?
o: Own-car business travel is repaid at a fair rate that managers may adjust from time to time
Staff using their own cars will be repaid for sensible travel costs once receipts are shown
Own-car business travel is repaid at J$55 per km, with a trip record approved by the manager
Staff who drive often should submit their claims promptly to their line manager
questions.why: A good policy gives a specific rate, the evidence needed and who approves, so every claim is treated the same way. Words such as 'fair', 'sensible' and 'often' leave too much to opinion, and 'should' makes a rule optional.

questions.q: At the owner's rate, what should Orville claim for the 240 km?
questions.why: Claim = distance x rate = 240 km x J$55 = J$13,200. Check the sum twice, and make sure the trip was approved and recorded.

questions.q: The owner wants managers to approve their own claims 'to save time'. Which principle should the policy keep?
o: Managers approve their own claims but report the total each year to the board
Claims under J$5,000 are exempt from approval by any other person
Claims are approved after payment, so that managers' work is not delayed
No one approves their own claim; it goes to the next level of management
questions.why: Approving your own claim removes the independent check, which is a core control. A faster route for urgent claims should be designed within the procedure, but the approver must be someone other than the claimant.

questions.q: What should the scope section of the new travel policy state?
o: The reasons why the owner has decided to introduce a travel policy this year
Whom and what it covers, such as contractors and part-time staff
The full list of steps that staff must follow when completing the claim form
The names of the managers who will approve claims in each department
questions.why: The scope says what and whom the policy covers, so that nobody is unsure whether it applies to them. Steps belong in the procedure, and approvers are shown by role in the roles section, not by name.

questions.q: What are the exporter's debtor days, and what do they show?
o: 20 days, so customers pay ten days before the 30-day terms end
40 days, so customers take 10 days longer to pay than the agreed terms
40 days, so the exporter is collecting faster than most hotels do
90 days, so customers pay at the end of the third month on average
questions.why: Credit sales per day = J$18,250,000 / 365 = J$50,000. Debtor days = J$2,000,000 / J$50,000 = 40 days. Against 30-day terms, this is 10 days late on average.

questions.q: What would the hotel's balance be if the new order were delivered, and what is the position against its limit?
o: J$870,000, which is J$70,000 inside its limit
J$220,000, which is within its limit
J$1,450,000, which is J$650,000 over its limit
J$870,000, which is J$70,000 over its limit
questions.why: New balance = J$650,000 + J$220,000 = J$870,000. The limit is J$800,000, so the balance would be J$70,000 over it. The credit policy should say what happens next.

questions.q: What should the credit policy say happens to an order that takes a customer over the limit?
o: It is held until an authorised person approves it or the balance falls
It is delivered at once, and the sales team asks the customer to pay later
It is cancelled and the customer is removed from the exporter's customer list
It is split into two orders so that each stays under the customer's limit
questions.why: A credit limit is a control only if it can stop an order. The policy should name who may approve an exception, so decisions are made by someone with authority. Splitting orders to avoid a limit is a breach.

questions.q: Under the delegation schedule, who approves writing off the J$95,000 debt?
o: The finance manager
The board
The managing director
The credit controller
questions.why: The finance manager's limit for write-offs is J$50,000. J$95,000 is above that and within the managing director's J$250,000 limit, so the managing director approves it. Only above J$250,000 does the board approve.

questions.q: The draft procedure allows buying without quotations up to J$600,000, but the national rules set a lower limit. What should the writer do?
o: Keep the J$600,000 limit, since the agency knows its own business best
Keep the limit, but ask department heads to record their reasons for each purchase
Lower the limit to match the national rule, as agency rules cannot be looser
Remove all limits and rely on the judgement of the department heads
questions.why: A public body's procedure works within national procurement rules and may add detail or tighter limits, but it cannot be looser. Check the current national rules when drafting.

questions.q: The draft does not say who acts when a budget holder is on leave. What is the best fix?
o: Name an acting role in the procedure and the delegation schedule
Allow any officer to approve in the budget holder's absence
Ask staff to wait until the budget holder returns before ordering
Let the finance team approve the purchase without telling anyone else
questions.why: A procedure must work every day, including when people are away. Naming the acting role (by job title) keeps approvals valid and keeps the control in place. Letting anyone approve removes the control.

questions.q: Which item should appear in the document-control box at the front of the finished procedure?
o: The names of the officers who wrote the first draft and their rank
The list of every purchase made under the previous procedure
A summary of the audit findings from the last three years
Version number, approval date, owner and next review date
questions.why: A document-control box lets staff see that they have the current version and who keeps it updated. This is the base of version control. Draft authors' names, past purchases and audit findings do not tell the reader whether the document is current.

questions.q: In the agency's flowchart, what does a diamond show?
o: The start or end of the procedure, where the flow begins
A decision, such as 'within limit?', with a yes arrow and a no arrow
A document, such as the requisition form used at that step
A step carried out by the finance team, such as paying the supplier
questions.why: A diamond is the decision shape: the flow splits into yes and no paths. Ovals show start or end, and rectangles show steps. Showing the 'no' path makes sure rejected requests are handled.

questions.q: What is the compliance rate for the sample of 150 claims?
questions.why: Compliant claims = 150 - 21 = 129. Compliance = 129 / 150 x 100 = 86%. The figure 14% is the non-compliance rate.

questions.q: Which finding needs the most urgent attention?
o: Seventeen small claims without receipts, as this is the largest number of breaches
The total of 21 breaches, as the sample is too small to show anything useful
The general manager's comment, as it is only an opinion and not a breach
Four claims approved by the person claiming, a breach of a key control
questions.why: The seventeen missing receipts are a training or process problem. Self-approval is more serious because it defeats the independent check; check whether the claims were genuine and report them. Count matters, but so does the kind of breach.

questions.q: What should the finance manager do about the 86% result?
o: Set a target, fix the causes, retest a new sample and report to the committee
Accept it as a good result, because most claims followed the policy rules
Dismiss the staff in the 21 claims and publish their names to the whole group
Stop testing, since this sample has already shown that the policy works well
questions.why: A compliance rate is a starting point: find the causes, put them right with training or system changes, and retest to show improvement. Results go to the committee. Naming and shaming does not fix a process problem.

questions.q: How should the finance manager respond to the general manager's suggestion that senior staff be exempt from the receipt rule?
o: Agree, since senior staff have earned the trust of the organisation
Agree, but only for claims that are paid from the senior staff's own budget
Apply the rule to all staff; take any exemption proposal to the committee
Agree for one quarter, and then test whether the exemption caused losses
questions.why: Rules that exempt leaders weaken the culture of compliance, because staff copy what senior people do. Any change to a policy must be approved by the body with authority, not decided informally.

questions.q: How should the printer and the photocopier be treated under the asset policy?
o: Both are fixed assets, since both are items of office equipment
Both are expenses, since neither costs more than J$200,000 each
The printer is an expense; the photocopier is recorded as a fixed asset
The printer is a fixed asset; the photocopier is an expense
questions.why: With a threshold of J$150,000, the printer (J$120,000) is below it and is charged as an expense. The photocopier (J$180,000) is above it and is capitalised and entered in the register.

questions.q: The board wants to review all its policies after eight years. What should come first?
o: List all policies and procedures with their owners and the date of each
Redraft every policy at once using a copy from a similar school
Ask the principal to approve each policy before any research is done
Delete the policies that no one has used in the last year
questions.why: You cannot review what you have not listed. A full list with owners and dates shows what exists, what is out of date and what to check first. Policies are then ranked by risk.

questions.q: The principal wants to buy equipment for J$140,000. What should happen?
o: She approves it herself, since the school needs the equipment urgently
She splits it into two orders of J$70,000 so that each is within her limit
She approves it and tells the committee at its next meeting
She asks the finance committee to approve it, as the amount is above her limit
questions.why: Her limit is J$100,000, so the purchase needs the committee's approval first. Splitting an order to stay under a limit is a breach of the control. Urgency should be handled through a defined fast route, not by bypassing the schedule.

questions.q: A manager says a written financial policy is unnecessary because 'everyone here knows the rules'. Which reply is best?
o: Written rules are needed only when the organisation is being audited by an outside firm
Written rules give the same answer to everyone, support staff who refuse improper requests and last when people change jobs
Unwritten rules are fine so long as the owner or the managing director still approves large payments
A written policy removes any need to train staff or check that the rules are followed
questions.why: A written policy gives consistency, authority and continuity. It also gives auditors and new staff something to test and learn from. It does not replace training or monitoring, and it is needed every day, not only at audit time.
